n: In the fifth year of the judges (about 87 BC), a clever, worldly man named Amlici stirs up conflict. He follows “the order of” Nehor — the same self-serving religion that led to Gideon’s murder.

f.w: after the order of the man that slew Gideon

n: Amlici gathers a powerful following and tries to have himself made king — exactly the danger Mosiah had warned about.

f.w: establish Amlici to be a king

n: Church members and other loyal citizens are alarmed, but they know the law: such a change must be decided by the voice of the people.
If Amlici won, he would strip away their religious freedoms, since his real aim was to destroy the church.
People gather throughout the land in groups for and against Amlici, with heated arguments.

f.g: “Wonderful” here means astonishing — remarkably intense disputes.

n: They cast their votes, and the results are given to the judges.
The people vote against Amlici; he is not made king. The system Mosiah set up works.

f.w: the voice of the people came against Amlici

n: Amlici’s opponents rejoice, but Amlici stirs his followers to anger.

f.g: Provoke, agitate.

n: His followers ignore the vote and crown Amlici anyway — rejecting the rule of law.

f.g: Formally set apart or install, here as king.

n: Amlici immediately orders his people to make war on their own countrymen to force them under his rule.

f.g: Bring them under his control.

n: His followers become known as Amlicites; the rest are called Nephites, or the people of God.

f.g: Many scholars note similarities with the “Amalekites” of Alma 21-24, possibly the same group under a variant spelling.

n: The Nephites prepare to defend themselves with every kind of weapon.

f.g: Scimitars — curved swords.

n: They organize their forces with captains at different levels, ready to meet the attack.

f.g: Senior military commanders.

n: Amlici arms his people and appoints leaders to wage war against their brethren.

f.g: A civil war — Nephite against Nephite.

n: The Amlicites attack at the hill Amnihu, east of the river Sidon near Zarahemla.

f.g: The major river of Nephite lands, flowing past Zarahemla.

n: As chief judge and governor, Alma personally leads the Nephite army into battle.

f.w: the chief judge and the governor

n: The battle is fierce; the Amlicites fight hard and many Nephites fall.

f.g: The hill Amnihu (verse 15).

n: But the Lord strengthens the Nephites, and the Amlicites begin to flee.

f.w: the Lord did strengthen the hand of the Nephites

n: The Nephites pursue all day. The death toll is staggering: 12,532 Amlicites and 6,562 Nephites — the price of one man’s ambition.

f.w: twelve thousand five hundred thirty and two
f.g: Mormon’s precise counts suggest records kept by Nephite officials.

n: Alma’s army camps for the night in the valley of Gideon, named for the faithful man Nehor killed.
Alma sends spies to follow the retreating Amlicites and learn their plans.

f.g: Scouts sent for military intelligence.

n: The scouts are named: Zeram, Amnor, Manti, and Limher.

f.g: A name also given to a hill and a land in Nephite territory.

n: The next day they rush back in alarm.

f.g: Their news is about to explain why.

n: In the land of Minon, toward the land of Nephi, they saw a huge Lamanite army — and the Amlicites had joined it.

f.g: Mentioned only here; it lay upriver (south) from Zarahemla, toward the land of Nephi.

n: The combined army was attacking Nephite settlers there, who fled toward Zarahemla. Unless the Nephite army hurried, the capital and their families would fall.

f.w: our fathers, and our wives, and our children

n: The Nephites break camp and head back toward Zarahemla.
As they cross the river Sidon, the vast Lamanite and Amlicite forces attack them.

f.w: as the sands of the sea
f.g: A common biblical image for a countless multitude.

n: The Nephites pray mightily for deliverance, and the Lord hears and strengthens them; their enemies begin to fall.
Alma and Amlici meet face to face and fight with swords.

f.g: Single combat between leaders — compare David and Goliath.

n: Mid-fight, Alma prays — not for glory, but for his life to be spared so he can keep serving and protecting his people.
Strengthened by the Lord, Alma kills Amlici.
Alma then confronts the Lamanite king, who retreats and sends his guards instead.

f.w: the king of the Lamanites fled
f.g: Unlike Alma, the Lamanite king will not risk himself in combat.

n: Alma and his guards fight the king’s guards until they kill or drive them back.

f.g: Alma’s personal bodyguards.

n: Alma clears the west bank of the river, throwing the dead into the water so his army has room to cross and fight.
Once the Nephites cross, the enemy — despite overwhelming numbers — breaks and runs.

f.g: Too many to count; the victory is credited to the Lord, not to numbers.

n: The enemy flees west and north into the wilderness beyond Nephite borders, with the Nephites in pursuit.

f.g: Away from Zarahemla and toward wild, unsettled territory.

n: Pursued from every side, they scatter into the wilderness of Hermounts, a region full of wild beasts.

f.g: A wilderness mentioned only here, known for dangerous animals.

n: Many die of their wounds in the wilderness and are eaten by animals and vultures. Their bones were later found and piled up — a grim memorial to the cost of rebellion.

f.g: Mormon, writing centuries later, may be drawing on the original record’s words.
